question.text: Find the orthogonal projection matrix that maps $\mathbf x\in \mathbb R^2$ onto the subspace spanned by an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda=5$ of the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 \end{bmatrix}.$
question.explanation:
The spectral decomposition of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ is given by

\[ A = \lambda_1 \mathbf u_1\cdot \mathbf u_1^T + \lambda_2 \mathbf u_2\cdot \mathbf u_2^T, \] where $\mathbf u_1$ and $\mathbf u_2$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalues $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2,$ respectively.

Moreover, $\mathbf u_i\cdot \mathbf u_i^T$ is the projection matrix corresponding to $\mathbf u_i.$

First, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to $\lambda=5.$ Computing $A-5I,$ we get

\begin{align*} A - 5 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 \end{bmatrix} - 5 \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -4 & 2 \\ 2 & -1 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

\begin{align*} M &= \left[ \begin{array}{cc|c} -4 & 2 & 0\\ 2 & 1 & 0 \end{array} \right] & R_2 & := R_2 + \dfrac12R_1 \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{cc|c} -4 & 2 & 0\\ 0& 0 & 0 \end{array} \right] \end{align*}

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, $x_2$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain $x_1=\dfrac12x_2.$ Hence, the general solution is

\[ \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac12x_2 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad x_2 \in \mathbb{R}. \]

Therefore, setting $x_2=2,$ we get the eigenvector

\[ \mathbf{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}, \]

where $\| \mathbf{v} \| = \sqrt{5}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}$ by its norm, we obtain the normalized eigenvector: \[ \mathbf{u} = \dfrac{\mathbf{v}}{\|\mathbf{v}\|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} \]

Finally, the required orthogonal projection matrix is given by

\begin{align*} \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{u}^T &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{5} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{5} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

question.text: Find the orthogonal projection matrix that maps $\mathbf x\in \mathbb R^2$ onto the subspace spanned by an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda=-1$ of the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix}.$
question.explanation:
The spectral decomposition of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ is given by

\[ A = \lambda_1 \mathbf u_1\cdot \mathbf u_1^T + \lambda_2 \mathbf u_2\cdot \mathbf u_2^T, \] where $\mathbf u_1$ and $\mathbf u_2$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalues $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2,$ respectively.

Moreover, $\mathbf u_i\cdot \mathbf u_i^T$ is the projection matrix corresponding to $\mathbf u_i.$

First, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to $\lambda=-1.$ Computing $A-(-1)I,$ we get

\begin{align*} A + 1 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix} + 1 \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

So, we have a system of linear equations which is already in row echelon form and has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, $x_2$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain $x_1=0.$ Hence, the general solution is

\[ \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad x_2 \in \mathbb{R}. \]

Therefore, setting $x_2=1,$ we get the eigenvector

\[ \mathbf{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}, \]

where $\| \mathbf{v} \| = 1.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}$ by its norm, we obtain the normalized eigenvector: \[ \mathbf{u} = \dfrac{\mathbf{v}}{\|\mathbf{v}\|} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \]

Finally, the required orthogonal projection matrix is given by

\begin{align*} \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{u}^T &= \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

question.text: Find the orthogonal projection matrix that maps $\mathbf x\in \mathbb R^2$ onto the subspace spanned by an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda=1$ of the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix} 10 & 12 \\ 12 & 17 \end{bmatrix}.$
question.explanation:
The spectral decomposition of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ is given by

\[ A = \lambda_1 \mathbf u_1\cdot \mathbf u_1^T + \lambda_2 \mathbf u_2\cdot \mathbf u_2^T, \] where $\mathbf u_1$ and $\mathbf u_2$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalues $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2,$ respectively.

Moreover, $\mathbf u_i\cdot \mathbf u_i^T$ is the projection matrix corresponding to $\mathbf u_i.$

First, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to $\lambda=1.$ Computing $A-1I,$ we get

\begin{align*} A - I &= \begin{bmatrix} 10 & 12 \\ 12 & 17 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 9 & 12 \\ 12 & 16 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

\begin{align*} M &= \left[ \begin{array}{cc|c} 9 & 12 & 0\\ 12 & 16 & 0 \end{array} \right] & R_2 & := R_2 + \left(-\dfrac43\right)R_1 \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{cc|c} 9 & 12 & 0\\ 0& 0 & 0 \end{array} \right] \end{align*}

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, $x_2$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain $x_1=-\dfrac43x_2.$ Hence, the general solution is

\[ \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac43x_2 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad x_2 \in \mathbb{R}. \]

Therefore, setting $x_2=3,$ we get the eigenvector

\[ \mathbf{v} = \begin{bmatrix} -4 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}, \]

where $\| \mathbf{v} \| = 5.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}$ by its norm, we obtain the normalized eigenvector: \[ \mathbf{u} = \dfrac{\mathbf{v}}{\|\mathbf{v}\|} = \dfrac{1}{5} \begin{bmatrix} -4 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix} \]

Finally, the required orthogonal projection matrix is given by

\begin{align*} \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{u}^T &= \dfrac{1}{5} \begin{bmatrix} -4 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \dfrac{1}{5} \begin{bmatrix} -4 & 3 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{25} \begin{bmatrix} -4 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} -4 & 3 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{25} \begin{bmatrix} 16 & -12 \\ -12 & 9 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

question.text:
Suppose that

$\qquad$ $\mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix} \quad$ and $\quad \mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}$

are eigenvectors of a $2 \times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ that correspond to the eigenvalues $\lambda_1=3$ and $\lambda_2=-2,$ respectively. Find the matrix $A.$
question.explanation:
The spectral decomposition of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ is given by

\[ A = \lambda_1 \mathbf u_1\cdot \mathbf u_1^T + \lambda_2 \mathbf u_2\cdot \mathbf u_2^T, \] where $\mathbf u_1$ and $\mathbf u_2$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalues $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2,$ respectively.

First, let's normalize our eigenvectors:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{u}_1 &= \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_1}{\| \mathbf{v}_1 \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix} \\[7pt] \mathbf{u}_2 &= \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_2}{\| \mathbf{v}_2 \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} \\[7pt] \end{align*}

Therefore, we have

\begin{align*} A &= \lambda_1 \mathbf{u}_1 \mathbf{u}_1^T + \lambda_2 \mathbf{u}_2 \mathbf{u}_2^T \\[5pt] &= 3 \cdot \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \end{bmatrix} + (-2) \cdot \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= 3 \cdot \dfrac{1}{5} \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \end{bmatrix} + (-2) \cdot \dfrac{1}{5} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{5} \left( 3 \cdot \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \end{bmatrix} + (-2) \cdot \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{5} \left( (3) \cdot \begin{bmatrix} 4 & -2 \\ -2 & 1 \end{bmatrix} + (-2) \cdot \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 \end{bmatrix} \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{5} \begin{bmatrix} 10 & -10 \\ -10 & -5 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -2 \\ -2 & -1 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

question.text:
Suppose that

$\qquad$ $\mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \quad$ and $\quad \mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix}$

are eigenvectors of a $2 \times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ that correspond to the eigenvalues $\lambda_1=5$ and $\lambda_2=-5,$ respectively. Find the matrix $A.$
question.explanation:
The spectral decomposition of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ is given by

\[ A = \lambda_1 \mathbf u_1\cdot \mathbf u_1^T + \lambda_2 \mathbf u_2\cdot \mathbf u_2^T, \] where $\mathbf u_1$ and $\mathbf u_2$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalues $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2,$ respectively.

First, let's normalize our eigenvectors:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{u}_1 &= \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_1}{\| \mathbf{v}_1 \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[7pt] \mathbf{u}_2 &= \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_2}{\| \mathbf{v}_2 \|} = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{5}} \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix} \\[7pt] \end{align*}

Therefore, we have

\begin{align*} A &= \lambda_1 \mathbf{u}_1 \mathbf{u}_1^T + \lambda_2 \mathbf{u}_2 \mathbf{u}_2^T \\[5pt] &= 5 \cdot \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix} + (-5) \cdot \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{5}} \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{5}} \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 4 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= 5 \cdot \dfrac{1}{5} \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix} + (-5) \cdot \dfrac{1}{20} \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 4 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{5} \left( 5 \cdot \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix} + (-5) \cdot \dfrac{1}{4} \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 4 \end{bmatrix} \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{5} \left( 5 \cdot \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix} + (-5) \cdot \dfrac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix} 4 & -8 \\ -8 & 16 \end{bmatrix} \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{5} \left( 5 \cdot \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix} + (-5) \cdot \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4 \end{bmatrix} \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{5} \begin{bmatrix} 15 & 20 \\ 20 & -15 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 4 \\ 4 & -3 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}
